flags.html: This question has no answer options in the PDF — it is open-ended. The key nonetheless reads "Answer: A". Taking the scale at face value, the score is 4, so presumably A was intended to be "4" in an earlier edition that had options.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119, Q133, Q137. Tests [[08 - Approach to Seizures]].
stem: Gerry, a 36-year-old carpenter, is brought to the ER by a friend of his, Joe. Joe explains that he and Gerry were working on a project when Gerry suddenly lost consciousness and started to jerk about wildly on the floor while turning blue. This lasted for about 15 seconds before Gerry's breathing returned to normal and he regained consciousness. Gerry says he feels fine now, but he's tired and a bit confused. He has no memory of the episode. What kind of seizure did Gerry just suffer?
answer:
The correct answer is C. In a tonic-clonic convulsion ("grand mal") the person loses consciousness suddenly, sometimes with a cry, and the body stiffens into tonic extensor rigidity. Breathing stops and the patient becomes cyanotic — the "turning blue" in the stem. A clonic phase of rhythmic muscular contraction follows. Injury, tongue biting and urinary incontinence may occur.

Afterwards the patient may be confused, drowsy or tired, with headache or muscle aches, and on exam bilateral neurologic deficits such as Babinski responses and hyperactive reflexes temporarily persist. The patient has amnesia for the seizure and no memory of an aura.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119, Q133, Q137. Tests [[08 - Approach to Seizures]].
stem: A mother brings in her 3-year old son Jake to the ED. She reports witnessing Jake have a seizure early today. Upon taking a further history, you ask Jake's mother to describe the seizure. She responds: "he suddenly seemed to lose consciousness, he arched his back and clenched his teeth and he had weird jerking movements back and forth." She further went on to detail that the seizure lasted somewhere between 5-10 minutes. There is no history of seizures and Jake is not on any medication. HR 100, RR 25, BP 106/61, T 38.5. Physical exam is unremarkable with no abnormal findings on the neurological exam. Currently, Jake appears well with no indications he is in a post-ictal state. What is the likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Simple vs. complex is the whole question:

Simple febrile seizureComplex febrile seizure
Typegeneralized tonic-clonicgenerally partial or focal in onset
Duration< 15 minutes ← Jake's 5-10 min> 15 minutes
Number in 24 honemultiple
Age6 months - 6 years ← Jake is 3—
Neuro statusnormaldevelopmental delay or neuro deficits may be present
Family historymay or may not be presentincludes nonfebrile seizures
Dispositionawake and alert → discharge with close pediatrician follow-upadmit with investigations; usually post-ictal

Jake is generalized, brief, singular, in the right age band, neurologically normal and not post-ictal → simple.

The other two seizure types for contrast: absence seizures — momentary lapses in awareness, staring, rhythmic blinking, often small clonic jerks, no postictal period. Myoclonic — rapid, recurrent, brief muscle jerks, bilateral/synchronous/asynchronous or unilateral, without loss of consciousness.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119, Q133, Q137. Tests [[08 - Approach to Seizures]].
stem: Typical febrile seizures present with all of the following, except?

options.html: History of similar event in the last 24 hours
No increased risk of developmental delay after the event

answer:
The correct answer is C. The general course of a typical febrile seizure:

  • Child is usually 6 months - 6 years old
  • No neurological abnormalities prior to the seizure
  • Develops a fever of ANY grade
  • Seizure of less than 15 min after fever onset (generalized, tonic-clonic)
  • Fever resolves with no neurological abnormalities
  • The child does not have another seizure within 24 hours of the first

If the child has another seizure within 24 hours, it is a Complex Febrile Seizure, and requires further investigation — which is exactly why C is the exception.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119, Q133, Q137. Tests [[08 - Approach to Seizures]].
stem: A 35-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with a history of recurrent episodes of uncontrolled muscle spasms that involve the whole body. During the episodes, the patient has a loss of consciousness and urinary incontinence. Which of the following types of seizure is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A. A generalized tonic-clonic seizure affects the whole brain and produces loss of consciousness, uncontrolled muscle spasms and urinary incontinence — all three given here.

  • Absence — brief lapses of consciousness with subtle movements such as blinking
  • Myoclonic — sudden, brief muscle contractions
  • Syncope — does not involve the characteristic muscle spasms and loss of consciousness pattern of a tonic-clonic seizure

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119, Q133, Q137. Tests [[08 - Approach to Seizures]].
stem: What is the term used to describe a type of febrile seizure that lasts longer than 15 minutes, occurs more than once within 24 hours, or is focal in nature?
answer: The workbook prints C, but by its own account the answer is B.

flags.title: The key contradicts itself and Q118/Q119
flags.html:
The key reads: "137. Answer: C. Status epilepticus. Febrile status epilepticus is a medical emergency... It is defined as a febrile seizure that lasts longer than 15 minutes, occurs more than once within 24 hours, or is focal in nature. Simple febrile seizures are typically brief and generalized... Complex febrile seizures may involve longer duration, focal features, or multiple episodes within 24 hours."

The key states the stem's definition twice — once for "febrile status epilepticus" and once for "complex febrile seizure". But that triad is the standard definition of a complex febrile seizure, and it is exactly what this section's own Q118 and Q119 teach. Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting ≥5 minutes (or recurrent seizures without recovery between them) — a different entity that is not febrile-specific. Answer B.

The key also invents a fourth term, "febrile focal seizures involve only one part of the body and may be a sign of an underlying neurological condition", which is not standard nomenclature.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q94-Q96, Q139. Tests [[11 - Neuroinfections]].
stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of fever and chills, a generalized headache and a stiff neck. There is a positive Kernig's sign. She is alert and oriented. CBC shows elevated WBCs. You are still waiting for blood cultures to return. Results of a lumbar puncture show cloudy CSF. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen to prescribe to this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A. This is acute bacterial meningitis, mostly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. Appropriate therapy: IV fluids, IV dexamethasone, and IV ceftriaxone + vancomycin, where the third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) covers N. meningitidis and vancomycin covers Strep. pneumoniae.

On the safety of the LP: this patient has no focal neurological signs (e.g. aphasia), so it is safe. LP is contraindicated if there is a mass in the brain (tumour or abscess) or if intracranial pressure is elevated, because it may cause brain herniation. See Q139 for the full empiric regimen including ampicillin and acyclovir.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q94-Q96, Q139. Tests [[11 - Neuroinfections]].
stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought into the emergency department by his parents. His parents are worried because over the past 3 days there has been vomiting, diarrhea, and purulent rhinorrhea. One day prior, he was difficult to arouse, and today they were not able to waken him. His temperature is currently 39°C. Is it safe to do a lumbar puncture on this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A — yes. It is mandatory to do an LP on all infants less than 3 months of age with fever.

The reason is the atypical presentation: meningitis in infants and young children presents non-specifically — for example GI upset without any signs of meningism, exactly as here. The key's rule of thumb: if in doubt, do an LP.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q94-Q96, Q139. Tests [[11 - Neuroinfections]].
stem: You suspect your patient has meningitis so you decide to do a lumbar puncture. What are the classical CSF findings of acute bacterial meningitis?

options.html: Increased protein, increased glucose, polymorphonuclear leukocytes
Increased protein, decreased glucose, polymorphonuclear leukocytes
Decreased protein, decreased glucose, polymorphonuclear leukocytes

answer:
The correct answer is C. Acute bacterial meningitis: increased protein, decreased glucose, polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

The cell type is the bacterial/viral discriminator: polymorphonuclear leukocytes indicate bacterial meningitis, while lymphocytes predominate in viral meningitis.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lectureMeta: Workbook Q94-Q96, Q139. Tests [[11 - Neuroinfections]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT an empiric first line medication for treatment of Meningitis in adults?
answer:
The correct answer is C — amoxicillin. The empiric regimen for bacterial meningitis in adults, with what each agent is there to cover:

DrugDoseCovers
Ceftriaxone2 g IV q12hH. influenzae, N. meningitidis, pan-susceptible Strep pneumo, MSSA
Vancomycin1 g IV q8hceftriaxone-resistant Strep pneumo, MRSA
Ampicillin2 g IV q4h — for immunocompromised adultsListeria

And if there are seizures or focal deficits, add acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for herpes simplex encephalitis — which is what option B of Q94 was testing.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q69, Q80-Q81. Tests [[02 - Brain Tumors]].
stem: Which of the following are the most common primary sources for brain metastases:
answer: The correct answer is A. Lung, breast, melanoma, renal cell are the most common primary sources of brain metastases. The discriminator across the options is melanoma being on the list and prostate/GI not.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q69, Q80-Q81. Tests [[02 - Brain Tumors]].
stem: Which of the following would most likely indicate a brain tumor?

options.html: Progression of neurologic symptoms over time

answer: The correct answer is E. The typical presentation of a brain tumour is an insidious onset of neurologic symptoms that progress over time. All of A-D can be caused by a tumour, but none of them is characteristic — it is the time course, not the symptom, that points to a mass lesion.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q69, Q80-Q81. Tests [[02 - Brain Tumors]].
stem: Which of the following is the most common primary brain tumour?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Gliomas are the most common primary brain tumours.

E is the trap, and it is a true statement: metastatic brain tumours are more common than primary brain tumours overall — but the question asks for the most common primary tumour, and a metastasis is by definition not primary. Compare meningioma and vestibular schwannoma.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q32, Q74-Q76. Tests [[05 - Movement Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is true regarding Parkinson's disease?

options.html: Intention tremor is a more common symptom than resting tremor
Low levels of dopamine lead to choreic dyskinesia

answer:
The correct answer is C. Parkinson's disease is caused by decreased dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, and its symptoms are the TRAP tetrad: resting Tremor, cogwheel Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability (see Q74).

Each distractor is inverted: patients have rigidity, not hypotonia (A); they gradually get worse with time (B); the tremor is at rest, not intention (D) — intention tremor is cerebellar; and choreic dyskinesias come from taking too much L-dopa, not from low dopamine (E) (see Q75).

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q32, Q74-Q76. Tests [[05 - Movement Disorders]].
stem: What are the main motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease?

options.html: Intention tremor, postural instability, shuffling gait and bradykinesia
Resting tremor, rigidity, dyskinesia and postural instability
Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability
Intention tremor, ataxia, rigidity and postural instability
Resting tremor, ataxia, spasticity and bradykinesia

answer:
The correct answer is C. The cardinal motor symptoms of PD are the TRAP mnemonic: resting Tremor, Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability.

The distractors each smuggle in a cerebellar sign (intention tremor, ataxia), an upper motor neuron sign (spasticity), or a treatment complication (dyskinesia — see Q75).

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q32, Q74-Q76. Tests [[05 - Movement Disorders]].
stem: What are some side effects of levodopa?
answer: The correct answer is B. Levodopa can cause dyskinesia, hallucinations, impulsivity, hypotension and somnolence, among others. The clinical task is finding an optimal dose that minimizes side effects while alleviating the motor symptoms — the trade-off Q32E gestures at.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q32, Q74-Q76. Tests [[05 - Movement Disorders]].
stem: A 63-year-old woman arrives in your clinic with a history of falls and bumping into objects and people. Upon examination you notice facial dystonia, axial rigidity, prominent postural instability and vertical gaze palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Secondary parkinsonism due to drug use

answer:
The correct answer is C. A typical presentation of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). Its features:

  • prominent postural instability with early falls
  • supranuclear gaze disturbance — which is what explains the bumping into objects and people
  • lid retraction
  • axial rigidity (as opposed to appendicular/peripheral — the contrast with PD)
  • facial dystonia
  • pseudobulbar palsy, cognitive impairment, and rarely tremor

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lecture: Motor neuron disease & the ALS team
lectureMeta: Workbook Q57-Q58, Q135-Q136. Tests [[01 - Multidisciplinary Care in ALS]].
stem: How is the diagnosis of ALS made?

options.html: Consistent history; i.e., relatively isolated motor symptoms that are progressive
Investigations to rule out alternative explanations
Exam demonstrates a combination of LMN signs and UMN signs in at least two regions

answer: The correct answer is D. All three are done to diagnose ALS — but C is the defining feature, because a combination of LMN and UMN signs in at least two regions is not generally found in other neurological conditions.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lecture: Motor neuron disease & the ALS team
lectureMeta: Workbook Q57-Q58, Q135-Q136. Tests [[01 - Multidisciplinary Care in ALS]].
stem: Which of the following is not a role of physiotherapy in managing a patient with ALS?

options.html: Protection of shoulders to prevent strain injury
Modify exercise routines as weakness progresses
All of the above are roles of physiotherapy

answer: The correct answer is E. Physiotherapy is involved in all of the above for ALS — respiratory hygiene, joint protection, exercise modification and edema management. Compare Q136 for the rest of the multidisciplinary team.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lecture: Motor neuron disease & the ALS team
lectureMeta: Workbook Q57-Q58, Q135-Q136. Tests [[01 - Multidisciplinary Care in ALS]].
stem: A 65-year-old male presents with progressive weakness and muscle wasting, particularly in his hands and arms, for the past 6 months. He reports difficulty with fine motor tasks such as writing and buttoning his shirt. His speech has also become slurred, and he has difficulty swallowing. On examination, you notice atrophy in his hands and fasciculations in his tongue. His reflexes are hyperactive, and he has a positive Babinski sign. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D. ALS is progressive degeneration and loss of motor neurons, causing weakness and atrophy that typically begins in the hands and feet and spreads over time. Other features: muscle cramps, fasciculations, spasticity, and difficulty with speech and swallowing.

What clinches it is the mix of signs, per Q57: LMN signs (hand atrophy, tongue fasciculations) alongside UMN signs (hyperreflexia, positive Babinski) — a combination multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis and Parkinson's disease do not produce.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lecture: Motor neuron disease & the ALS team
lectureMeta: Workbook Q57-Q58, Q135-Q136. Tests [[01 - Multidisciplinary Care in ALS]].
stem: Which of the following allied health care professionals is NOT part of the multidisciplinary team involved in the care of a patient with ALS?

options.html: All of the above are part of the multidisciplinary team involved in the care of a patient with ALS.

answer: The correct answer is E. ALS affects multiple systems — motor, respiratory and swallowing — so it requires a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach. The team typically includes an occupational therapist, speech-language pathologist, physical therapist, nutritionist, social worker and others as needed, each with a role in maintaining function, managing symptoms, and providing emotional support to the patient and family. Compare Q58 for physiotherapy's specific contribution.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q86-Q88. Tests [[03 - Pediatric Neurology]], [[04 - Non-Mendelian Genetics]].
stem: Which of the following statements regarding cerebral palsy is true?

options.html: In terms of quality of life, children generally rate slightly lower than parents
99% of children with abnormal motor signs at their first birthday will outgrow findings by the 7th year
Many children with non-specific motor findings in infancy will evolve to a clear CP pattern by the age of 2 years
Increased birth weight is a risk factor

answer:
The correct answer is D. Every distractor is the correct fact with a number or direction flipped:

  • A — parents generally rate quality of life slightly lower than children do (the reverse of the option)
  • B — CP is diagnosed after the age of 2, not 8
  • C — 50%, not 99%, of children with abnormal motor signs at their first birthday will outgrow the findings by age 7
  • E — decreased birth weight is the risk factor

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q86-Q88. Tests [[03 - Pediatric Neurology]], [[04 - Non-Mendelian Genetics]].
stem: Prader-Willi Syndrome and Angelman Syndrome are both associated with deletions of the same bands from the long arm of chromosome 15. However, the physical expression associated with each disorder is very different. This is an example of:
answer:
The correct answer is A — imprinting. The same locus produces two different diseases depending on which parent contributed it:

  • Angelman syndrome — paternal uniparental disomy 15 (2 copies from father, none from mother)
  • Prader-Willi syndrome — maternal uniparental disomy 15 (2 copies from mother, none from father)

Uniparental disomy arises from one or more nondisjunction events in the gametes.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q86-Q88. Tests [[03 - Pediatric Neurology]], [[04 - Non-Mendelian Genetics]].
stem: Huntington's Chorea is an example of which genetic inheritance?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Huntington's disease is a neuropsychiatric disorder with autosomal dominant inheritance; its gene is on the short arm of chromosome 4.

The psychiatric course is worth knowing: manifestations range from mild depression, anxiety and irritability to frank hallucinations and delusions, all of which may precede the onset of choreiform movements. Dementia occurs in the terminal phase and is characterized by impaired cognition without a language disorder.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q104-Q108. Tests [[07 - Red Eye and Ocular Trauma]].
stem: A 25-year-old male comes into the emergency department with a bruised, bloody eye. On history, he claims he was "minding his own business" at a bar when someone punched him. A CT scan reveals a teardrop sign. Which of the following bones of the orbit have likely been injured?

options.html: Roof - frontal bone & lesser wing of sphenoid
Inferior wall - maxilla, zygomatic & palatine bones
Lateral wall - zygomatic & greater wing of sphenoid bone

answer:
The correct answer is D. The medial and inferior walls of the orbit are relatively weak. If the inferior wall fractures in a "blowout fracture", orbital fat herniates into the maxillary sinus, creating the "teardrop sign" on CT.

The inferior wall is made up of the maxilla, zygomatic and palatine bones, and forms the roof of the maxillary sinus — which is why the fat has somewhere to go. B and C are the same wall/bone confusion: ethmoid is the medial wall, not the inferior.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q104-Q108. Tests [[07 - Red Eye and Ocular Trauma]].
stem: A 62-year-old male is experiencing purulent discharge from his eyes. He says his eyes are burning and stinging. In the morning, he wakes up and is unable to open his eyes because they are crusted shut. His corneas are clear, intraocular pressure is normal, and pupils are normal sized and normally reactive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The single most useful fact in this cluster of questions: there is no pain in conjunctivitis — it is the only one of conjunctivitis, iritis, acute glaucoma and corneal ulcer that doesn't cause pain. It can still be very uncomfortable (burning, stinging). And in conjunctivitis the pupil is normal size, the cornea is clear, and the intraocular pressure is normal — all three given here.

Then sub-type by discharge:

  • Bacterial — purulent discharge ← this patient
  • Viral — watery, red eye, foreign body sensation, photophobia
  • Allergic — itching predominates
  • Chlamydial — see Q105

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q104-Q108. Tests [[07 - Red Eye and Ocular Trauma]].
stem: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency clinic with copious discharge from his right eye. He wakes up in the morning, unable to open his eyes because they are crusted shut. He feels like there is a foreign body in his eye, but upon examination you do not see any foreign object. However, you do notice conjunctival follicles upon slit lamp examination. He says his family doctor gave him topical antibiotics a week ago, but has seen no improvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Chlamydial conjunctivitis usually presents with copious sticky discharge, and crucially it does not respond to topical antibiotics — which is what makes bacterial conjunctivitis less likely, since that can be treated topically (tobramycin, gentamicin, sodium sulamyd).

Chlamydial conjunctivitis must be treated with oral antibiotics such as tetracycline, erythromycin or doxycycline. The failed week of topical therapy in the stem is the diagnostic clue.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q104-Q108. Tests [[07 - Red Eye and Ocular Trauma]].
stem: A 24-year-old female comes to your family medical practice complaining of rapid onset pain in her right eye. In addition, she is sensitive to light and can't see very well out of her right eye. On examination, you see a hazy cornea, a small pupil, and flare and cells in the anterior chamber. Her intraocular pressure is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
answer:
The correct answer is E. This is acute iritis (anterior uveitis). Iritis is a type of intraocular inflammation, so cells and flare (protein) are seen in the anterior chamber — that finding is the diagnosis.

Treatment: topical or oral steroids to decrease the inflammation, plus cycloplegic drops (pupil dilators) such as topical homatropine. Also promptly refer to ophthalmology.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q104-Q108. Tests [[07 - Red Eye and Ocular Trauma]].
stem: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the ED with nausea and vomiting. Upon review of systems you elicit that he is also experiencing significant pain in his left eye. He also complains of decreased vision and colored halos around lights. You notice his left eye is red, and his pupil is fixed and dilated and nonresponsive to light. The most appropriate next step is:

options.html: Prescribe him some antiemetics and send him home.
Evaluate his intraocular pressure with tonopen.
Write him a script for topical timolol to decrease aqueous humor production by the ciliary.

answer:
The correct answer is B. The picture is acute angle-closure glaucoma — but to confirm it you must measure the intraocular pressure (IOP), and the question asks for the next step, not the treatment.

IOP can be measured with a tonopen or with Goldmann applanation on the slit lamp. Although Goldmann applanation is the gold standard, tonopens are used more often in the emergency room. Only once you have confirmed acute angle-closure do you prescribe an IOP-lowering drug such as topical timolol (D) or arrange definitive laser iridotomy (C).

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q104-Q108. Tests [[07 - Red Eye and Ocular Trauma]].
stem: You are evaluating a 20-year-old female for suspected corneal ulcer due to long term contact lens wear. Which of the following will you use to stain the damaged corneal epithelium, so that you can visualize the corneal ulcer under the slit lamp?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Fluorescein is a yellow dye applied to the eye; under the blue light of the slit lamp, damaged corneal epithelium appears yellow. See corneal ulcer.

Every other option is a drug from a neighbouring question: homatropine is the cycloplegic from Q106, timolol and acetazolamide are glaucoma medications from Q107/Q109.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q9, Q109-Q110, Q115-Q116. Tests [[06 - Monocular Vision Impairment]].
stem: Macular degeneration leads to which of the following vision changes?

options.html: Blurring of the entire visual field

answer:
The correct answer is E. The macula is the area in the centre of the retina that includes the fovea and is responsible for central vision, so degeneration there makes reading difficult or impossible. Motion detection is preserved, because the peripheral rods still work — which rules out D.

The other options are the other diseases' signatures:

  • Blurring of the entire field → cataracts, from abnormal protein deposits
  • Tunnel vision / loss of peripheral vision → glaucoma, because the large ganglion cells from the peripheral retina are the first damaged when high pressure compresses the optic nerve

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q9, Q109-Q110, Q115-Q116. Tests [[06 - Monocular Vision Impairment]].
stem: Which of the following is not a class of glaucoma medication?
answer: The correct answer is B. The 5 general classes of glaucoma medication are: beta blockers, alpha receptor AGONISTS, miotics, prostaglandin analogues, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Antagonists are not among them — the question turns on the single word.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q9, Q109-Q110, Q115-Q116. Tests [[06 - Monocular Vision Impairment]].
stem: A 67-year-old man visits his ophthalmologist for his routine follow up of his diabetic retinopathy. This year, you are suspicious he has progressed from non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy to proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Which of the following seen on examination would make you suspicious of this progression?
answer: The correct answer is C. The hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy is the formation of new vessels. Everything else listed can appear in non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy — only neovascularization marks the transition.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q9, Q109-Q110, Q115-Q116. Tests [[06 - Monocular Vision Impairment]].
stem: What is the (soft) upper limit for a normal cup to disc ratio?
answer: The correct answer is B — 0.5. Although any C/D ratio can be found in a healthy eye, a range of 0.3 to 0.5 is typically considered normal — which is why the stem says "soft" limit.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q9, Q109-Q110, Q115-Q116. Tests [[06 - Monocular Vision Impairment]].
stem: The leading cause of irreversible blindness in adults over 52 years old is:
answer: The correct answer is A. The operative word is irreversible: cataracts can be reversed surgically, whereas the course of macular degeneration can only be slowed — with anti-VEGF injections for "wet" macular degeneration and antioxidants for "dry".

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q112-Q113. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology]].
stem: A cataract in one eye that develops early in childhood that is not fixed during the critical period leads to which of the following?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Amblyopia means cortical blindness. When one eye is deprived of input — for example by a cataract — the other eye gradually takes over all of the cortical representation. If the abnormality is not reversed during the critical period, permanent cortical blindness develops.

  • Stereopsis — the word for depth perception (a normal function, not a deficit)
  • Strabismus — the eyes are not properly aligned (see Q112)
  • Hemianopsia — decreased vision or blindness in half the visual field, usually on one side of the vertical midline

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q112-Q113. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology]].
stem: Strabismic amblyopia is due to:

options.html: A difference in refraction between the eyes; the eye with poor vision is suppressed.
A deprivation of vision in one eye due to a cataract.
A lesion in the occipital lobe.
A defect in the optic nerve causing blindness in one eye.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Strabismus is misalignment of the two eyes, typically from lack of coordination of the extraocular muscles. Amblyopia is a type of cortical blindness — one eye is not represented in the visual cortex, and the patient never develops higher-order visual functions such as binocular vision and depth perception.

In strabismic amblyopia the two combine: because the eyes are misaligned, vision from one eye is suppressed to prevent double vision, and the bad eye loses its representation in the visual cortex. If the critical period passes without realignment, the cortex is no longer plastic and the patient stays blind in that eye even if the eye itself is restored to normal.

Treatment: patch the "good" eye to force use of the bad one and strengthen its extraocular muscles; surgery may be required to realign the eye. Note A is refractive amblyopia and B is deprivation amblyopia (Q13) — different subtypes, not wrong facts.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Brain Tumours, Movement Disorders, Pediatrics & Ophthalmology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q112-Q113. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology]].
stem: You are evaluating a patient for double vision. You notice the patient's right eye is always pointing towards their nose. You describe this eye as being:
answer: The correct answer is A. Esotropia refers to an in-turned eye (eso- = inward, -tropia = a manifest deviation). Exo- is outward; a -phoria is a latent deviation that only appears when fusion is broken, which is why B and D are wrong even with the right direction.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63, Q66-Q67, Q123-Q124. Tests [[04 - Hearing Loss]].
stem: A 61-year-old woman arrives in your clinic complaining of hearing loss. Upon performing the Weber test you find that sound localizes to the right ear. You get a positive Rinne test (AC>BC) for both ears. What is the most likely cause of the patient's hearing loss?

options.html: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss primarily affecting the right ear
Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss primarily affecting the left ear
Conductive hearing loss of the right ear
Conductive hearing loss of the left ear

answer:
The correct answer is B. Two tests, applied in sequence:

  • Weber localizing to the right ear is ambiguous on its own — it means either conductive loss of the right ear or asymmetric sensorineural loss primarily affecting the left ear.
  • A positive Rinne (AC > BC) is the normal result, which excludes conductive hearing loss — and it is positive bilaterally, so neither ear has a conductive problem.

That leaves asymmetric sensorineural loss of the left ear.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63, Q66-Q67, Q123-Q124. Tests [[04 - Hearing Loss]].
stem: What is the most common cause of bacterial otitis externa (swimmers' ear)?
answer: The correct answer is C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common organism causing swimmer's ear, followed by Staph aureus. See otitis externa.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63, Q66-Q67, Q123-Q124. Tests [[04 - Hearing Loss]].
stem: Name two treatments for sensorineural hearing loss.
answer:
Hearing aids and cochlear implants.

  • Hearing aids amplify sounds at pre-set frequencies to overcome hearing loss in that range. However, amplification cannot improve sound clarity — which is the limitation that matters.
  • Cochlear implants stimulate CN VIII directly, bypassing the hair cells.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63, Q66-Q67, Q123-Q124. Tests [[04 - Hearing Loss]].
stem: The ______ attaches to the malleus and is innervated by _____, and functions to dampen sound waves.
answer:
The correct answer is D. The two dampening muscles pair with the bone they attach to and the nerve that supplies them:

  • Tensor tympani → malleus → CN V3
  • Stapedius → stapes → CN VII

Both function to dampen sound waves — hence the hyperacusis in a CN VII lesion (Q30). The name gives the attachment away in each case.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63, Q66-Q67, Q123-Q124. Tests [[04 - Hearing Loss]].
stem: Which of the following is correct regarding the auditory/Eustachian/Pharyngotympanic tube:

options.html: Connects the inner ear to the nasopharynx
It is more horizontal in adults than in infants and children
It is commonly infected in otitis media

answer:
The workbook prints A, but its own explanation shows the answer is C.

The three facts, correctly stated:

  • The tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx — not the inner ear
  • It is more horizontal in infants and children than in adults, which is why they get more ear infections
  • It is commonly infected in otitis media ✓

flags.title: The key contradicts itself
flags.html:
The key reads: "124. Answer: A. Connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx b) Is more horizontal in infants and children than adults c) True, it is commonly infected in otitis media".

Option A as printed says "inner ear", which the key's own correction ("middle ear") makes false. The key then explicitly marks C as "True". So C is the correct answer and the printed letter is a slip.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q64, Q68, Q70-Q72. Tests [[05 - Vertigo]]. Q70-Q72 are one BPPV case.
stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of Meniere's disease?

options.html: Sensorineural hearing loss in the low frequency range (125 Hz to 1000 Hz)
Sudden attacks of vertigo preceded by tinnitus

answer:
The correct answer is E. Meniere's disease is characterized by all of: sensorineural hearing loss in the low frequency range, sudden attacks of vertigo lasting minutes to hours preceded by tinnitus, aural fullness, and fluctuating hearing loss.

The low-frequency detail distinguishes it from presbycusis (high frequencies, Q6), and the minutes-to-hours duration distinguishes it from BPPV (seconds, Q70).

lectureMeta: Workbook Q64, Q68, Q70-Q72. Tests [[05 - Vertigo]]. Q70-Q72 are one BPPV case.
stem: Which one of the following matches the vestibular organ with its proper function?

options.html: anterior and posterior semicircular canals – sense head position relative to gravity
horizontal semicircular canals – sense linear acceleration
otoliths – sense nodding of head forward and backward
anterior and posterior semicircular canals – sense shaking of head right and left
horizontal semicircular canals – sense shaking of head right and left

answer:
The correct answer is E. The division of labour:

  • Semicircular canals sense angular motion — horizontal canals for shaking the head right and left; anterior and posterior canals for nodding forward and backward
  • Otoliths sense linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity

Every distractor swaps a canal function with an otolith function or swaps the two canal planes.

stem:
Refer to the following case for questions 70-72: A 65-year-old woman presents to your clinic complaining of episodic vertigo over the past three weeks. Her initial episode occurred when she was lying down in bed and rolled over from her right to left side. She stated that the vertigo woke her up and felt like the "room was spinning." The episodes only last for seconds and are aggravated by very specific head movements, such as when looking up to reach for something from her cupboard. She claims the vertigo is associated with nausea but no vomiting.

What is the most likely cause of her vertigo?
answer: The correct answer is C. Episodic vertigo, aggravated by very specific head movements and lasting only seconds is BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo). The duration is the discriminator: much shorter than Meniere's, which lasts minutes to hours (Q64).

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q64, Q68, Q70-Q72. Tests [[05 - Vertigo]]. Q70-Q72 are one BPPV case.
stem: How would you confirm her diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. BPPV is diagnosed on a positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver.

How it is performed: patient sits upright with legs extended; the head is rotated 45° to the right; the clinician helps them lie back quickly with the head held in ~20° of extension; the eyes are observed for about 45 seconds.

The characteristic positive finding is a direction-specific rotatory nystagmus with a 2-5 second latency. The nystagmus is of limited duration (15-20 seconds), reverses direction when the patient sits up, and is fatiguable — repeated testing produces less and less nystagmus.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q64, Q68, Q70-Q72. Tests [[05 - Vertigo]]. Q70-Q72 are one BPPV case.
stem: How is this condition treated?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Treatment options for BPPV include reassurance, habituation exercises, particle repositioning manoeuvre, or surgery.

C is excluded because a low sodium diet is the Meniere's treatment, not a BPPV one — which is what makes D rather than E correct.

lecture: Neurology in medical illness: Wernicke's encephalopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q126-Q127. Tests [[02 - Integration of Medicine and Neurology]]. Q126-Q127 are one case.
stem:
Questions 126 and 127 are based on the following scenario: A 40-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department after her family found her in a confused state at her home. Upon initial evaluation, she is found to be disoriented and lethargic. CN nerve exam revealed horizontal nystagmus and diplopia but was otherwise normal. On motor and sensory exam reflexes, power, and sensation was normal throughout. She did exhibit bilateral dysmetria with finger to nose and heel to shin testing and had a severely ataxic gait. On history it is found that the patient has undergone roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, there is no history of head trauma.

Where does this lesion localize to?

options.html: Symptoms cannot be localized to a single part of the nervous system.

answer:
The correct answer is E. The symptoms are most in keeping with Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is a generalized dysfunction of multiple systems rather than a single focal lesion.

The classic triad is all present: confusion (disoriented, lethargic), ophthalmoplegia (horizontal nystagmus, diplopia) and ataxia (bilateral dysmetria, ataxic gait). The roux-en-Y gastric bypass is the risk factor — malabsorptive surgery causing thiamine deficiency.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Hearing, Vertigo & Neurology in Medical Illness
lecture: Neurology in medical illness: Wernicke's encephalopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q126-Q127. Tests [[02 - Integration of Medicine and Neurology]]. Q126-Q127 are one case.
stem: What would be the most useful diagnostic lab/imaging test for the condition you are suspecting?
answer: The correct answer is D. Since the suspicion is Wernicke's encephalopathy, thiamine is the key cause of the condition and blood thiamine levels are the targeted test. (Clinically, treatment is given empirically without waiting for the result.)

stem:
Match the following structures in the brainstem with their corresponding function. (The options in the right hand column can be used once, more than once, or not at all, but all of the options on the left must be used once):

StructureFunction
i. Cerebral PedunclesA) Cause your head to turn toward an auditory stimulus
ii. Pontine NucleiB) Relay centers for corticopontocerebellar pathway
iii. Gracile tubercleC) Cause your head to turn toward a visual stimulus
iv. Inferior colliculusD) Contain corticospinal tract fibers
v. Superior colliculusE) Release endorphins in response to pain stimulus
vi. Cuneate tubercleF) Carry sensory information from the dorsal column
vii. Periaqueductal gray matter
viii. Medullary pyramids
answer:
i-D, ii-B, iii-F, iv-A, v-C, vi-F, vii-E, viii-D.

StructureFunction
Cerebral pedunclescontain corticospinal tract fibres
Pontine nucleirelay centres for the corticopontocerebellar pathway
Gracile tuberclecarries dorsal column sensory information — from the lower limbs
Inferior colliculusturns the head toward an auditory stimulus
Superior colliculusturns the head toward a visual stimulus
Cuneate tuberclecarries dorsal column sensory information — from the upper limbs
Periaqueductal grayreleases endorphins in response to pain
Medullary pyramidscontain corticospinal tract fibres

The key's organizing logic: the corticospinal tract travels through the cerebral peduncles in the midbrain and the pyramids in the medulla — at which point most fibres decussate (hence D used twice). Inferior and superior colliculi in the midbrain turn us toward a sudden stimulus — inferior to auditory, superior to visual. The gracile and cuneate tubercles in the medulla contain nuclei receiving dorsal column input — gracile from the lower limbs, cuneate from the upper (hence F used twice).

stem:
Match the following area in the brain with the description of a lesion of that structure. There may be multiple deficits (column 2) for a given lesion (column 1), such that all of the options are used once. The number of deficits is indicated in brackets after the location of the lesion.

LesionDeficit
i. Amygdala (1 deficit)A) Inability to remember which cup a coin was placed under 5 sec. ago
ii. Frontal lobe (3 deficits)B) Inability to name objects presented visually on the patient's left side
iii. Right parietal cortex (1)C) Lack of emotional response triggered by seeing parents' faces
iv. Corpus Callosum (2)D) Cannot remember new people they meet
v. Hippocampus (2)E) Lack of initiative and decision-making ability
F) Neglect the left half of objects
G) Cannot coordinate left and right hemispheres of the brain
H) Inability to do mental math
I) Cannot convert short-term memories into long-term memories
answer:
i-C; ii-A, E, H; iii-F; iv-B, G; v-D, I.

LesionDeficitsWhy
AmygdalaCthe amygdala makes us recognize that certain people are familiar. Without that sense of familiarity you can see that your parents look exactly as they should, but something is not quite right — the basis of the delusion that they are imposters or have been replaced
Frontal lobeA, E, Hinvolved in decision-making, initiative, and working memory — remembering numbers while adding them in your head, words as you read a sentence, or which cup an object went under
Right parietal cortexFthe parietal lobe handles attention, so a right lesion causes neglect of the left half of objects
Corpus callosumB, Git connects and coordinates the two hemispheres; severed, an object perceived in the right visual cortex cannot reach the language areas if they are on the left (the most common location)
HippocampusD, Iit converts short-term memories into long-term ones, which is what remembering a new acquaintance requires
